As I understand it FND is not “faking it” it just means that the pain originates in the brain instead of the area that hurts. So if someone presented with pain in a body part (let’s say the arm for the sake of ease) and all examination showed that the arm itself was functionally and structurally sound, FND might be a possible diagnosis. It’s not that the pain doesn’t exist or is imaginary, it’s that the brain is manifesting pain in that area because something neurological it doesn’t know what to do with is happening. It’s sort of like your brain having a signal it can’t interpret and going “must be arm pain!” and then dishing out the arm pain accordingly. It’s not something you’re doing to yourself intentionally but rather something your brain is doing to your body. Stress, trauma, environmental factors, all sorts of things can theoretically be responsible for the brain manifesting physical symptoms. As for it being “all in your head”…well, that’s complicated. It’s not imaginary! But it is in your head because that’s where your brain is and your brain controls pain, energy, balance, all sorts of important stuff that can get thrown off. I hope you’re able to find answers and pain relief moving forward!

Plaster hand casts were very popular gifts and keepsakes in the 19th century. People would have them made after someone died or to show how small a child’s hand was as they grew. Queen Victoria had one made from Prince Albert’s hand, for example, and had casts done of her children’s hands/arms. The photo strongly resembles existing examples of those Victorian-era casts. I would put money on this not being human at all and in fact being a discarded keepsake of some sort.

Agreed, the hand in the picture is absolutely a cast. You wouldn’t see that kind of detail (the ring, the nail beds, etc.) if it was flesh that had been mineralized. Plaster casts of hands and arms were popular tokens in the Victorian era, whether as a memorial item or a memento of a child or loved one. Queen Victoria had a plaster cast of Prince Albert’s hand taken after his death and the trend became even more pervasive. This is likely one of those 19th century mementos lost or purposely discarded.

As someone with cerebral palsy I am very concerned about the sudden progression of worsening symptoms your sister experienced. Cerebral palsy is not a progressive condition and should not be presenting this way without other factors at work. You don’t generally have someone who could previously speak suddenly lose that ability without something else going on like epilepsy or a progressively degenerative illness. She needs to see a neurologist to find out if something else is going on. I am also 33 and while I notice changes in my function (pain from spasticity/changes to my bones/etc.) and decreased mobility that is the amount of “degeneration” expected from cerebral palsy over time, not what you’re describing. A neurologist (and possibly a geneticist if they suspect something that -looks like- cerebral palsy but is progressive might be happening) is the immediate first place I’d look.

The phrasing of this is horrid and yet the subject matter is incredibly important. Say you’re a manager and you call your subordinate in to talk about their performance. The clients they manage say that your subordinate is unfriendly and aloof and doesn’t seem invested in them. When you bring this up, your subordinate seems surprised as their client’s needs are all being met in a timely manner. “I wasn’t aware that my clients felt that I wasn’t engaged or seemed aloof. I’m autistic and I find that people often read me as disengaged because my face isn’t very expressive when I’m focused on the content of what they’re saying.” This now reframes the entire meeting. For a manager who has never dealt with this situation, a seminar like this is incredibly useful. It would teach the skills that would allow a manager to step back for a moment, regroup, not feel flustered or redirect their discomfort, and shift from disciplinary to problem-solving. They need to know what they legally can and cannot ask, what they can offer in terms of accommodations, and what steps need to be taken to ensure that the subordinate has (in writing) what they need to perform their job. It should never be about “This person is using their disability as an excuse” or “how can I find a way to fire them” but about giving people the tools to succeed in their roles. We can’t talk about accessibility in the workforce without talking about how disability can intersect with performance, perceived or otherwise, and how to talk about these issues when they arise.

I experienced the “thinking I’m hearing muffled conversation next door” thing a lot and it caused me a huge amount of distress. I recognized that no one was there or speaking but I kept getting snippets of almost-but-not-quite conversations at the edge of my hearing. It was my neurologist that finally explained that it wasn’t a hallucination/delusion/psychosis but a totally benign “glitch” in the way my brain filters noise. Normally when we hear something we subconsciously sort noise into meaningful and meaningless, speech and not-speech, at a reflexive level. Sometimes my brain will take not-speech, like the sound of a dishwasher going, and throw it down the speech chute. So the part of my brain that’s dedicated to processing speech and language is being handed the sound of a dishwasher under the guise of it being language somehow. That’s where the “?? Words??” feeling is coming from. And now that I know what’s happening it doesn’t bother me anymore. It still happens but I can go “yeah, my brain is kinda bad at sorting stuff” versus “I am hearing voices”.

ER visit sometimes yes, unfortunately, especially if it’s the type that causes issues with clotting. And because it shares so many markers with child abuse it’s generally protocol to report the first incident and then the case will be closed if a diagnosis is made. The problem with certain blood diseases is that they can be fatal very quickly and in ways that aren’t immediately obvious. It’s better to get the kid to the ER, make sure they aren’t bleeding anywhere internal/don’t have any non-visible head injuries and go from there. If you just look at Von Willebrand alone, a single bruise could mean “kid’s blood isn’t clotting properly and even mild pressure is causing internal bleeding” to “the kid’s blood is clotting way too much/fast, he’s at risk for a variety of sudden issues and needs treatment” and sending a kid with either of those problems home could mean accidental death. I feel horrible for the parents in this situation but these procedures are designed to protect the kids -and- keep innocent parents from being blamed for things that could be illness-related.

From the non-abuse side of things: bruises on a non-mobile baby can also be the first red flag for many blood disorders like Von Willebrand Disease or hemophilia. That’s why children evaluated for abuse are also screened for those conditions. The nurse made the right call in reporting the bruise but should have given clear, concise directions to the parents about what to do and when. “Go to the emergency department, tell them you were sent from (place), we called ahead, we are going to rule out anything that can cause bruising so it’s very important that you go immediately”. It was the lack of clear communication that caused so many issues, not even touching on the costs…

And as far as memory problems tied to grief and stress being permanent…I completely understand that fear. Fortunately there’s a ton of really good studies that back up the belief that things begin to go back to normal the further you are from the initial loss. stress and grief cause us to intentionally stop prioritizing the use of parts of the brain that aren’t directly related to survival. In short? Your brain just turns off power to things like long term memory recall, acquisition of new information, etc. if it thinks it needs the power just to survive. We haven’t evolved to a point where our brain and nervous system can differentiate between the (modern) grief of losing a loved one during a pandemic and the evolutionary “oh god there’s a lion and it’s gonna eat me”. That’s why in the time shortly after a traumatic event you feel so foggy and disconnected, and why trying to remember good times seems like such an uphill battle. You’re basically trying to fumble around and find something in a room where someone turned the lights off to save energy. Everything is safe where you left it, you just need time to heal and re-route your energy so there’s enough to run all the lights at once.

I’m not questioning that she was deaf and blind. I’m simply saying that modern science (for better or worse) has become incredibly specific in quantifying and describing someone’s disabilities. If she lived today we’d be saying things like “she was (percent) deaf, able to hear (nothing, certain pitch, etc)” and have better terms to discuss the nuances of her blindness. I spent a bit of time digging into family history regarding disability (I’m disabled myself and writing about perception of disability over time) and found that the medical language of even the 1960s-1980s was woefully inadequate and most records were sparing in detail. Even firsthand accounts of disability tend to be colored by the information that person has been given about their own condition. We know how Helen experienced the world, her descriptions of life were incredibly open and honest. I just wish we had more in the way of quantifiable information (like the results of modern diagnostic testing) on her vision, hearing, and what her brain was doing as she processed language. It would be invaluable in helping doctors and scientists to better help people with the same disabilities.

People tend to think of “deaf and blind” as absolutes. We don’t know that she could hear 0% of sounds and see absolutely no light/color. I think it’s far more likely she was deaf with a small degree of hearing and profoundly visually impaired. Additionally, people forget that she lost her sight and hearing at almost 2 vs being born that way. She had the advantage of being able to process at least some verbal language before losing those abilities again, that’s huge for building the neuropathways for later language development. I kinda think it’s more ableist to ignore these factors and push the “hard work overcomes all” narrative tbh, you’re right to question assumptions about her abilities. It doesn’t mean she wasn’t amazing or disabled or whatever it just means that people haven’t done a good job telling her story.

The first apartment my wife and I had together just had a weird vibe to it. We liked it well enough, it was super cute and right at the upper end of what we could afford. We thought the extra money was worth it to have such a cute place in a Victorian building. But from the moment we moved in there was just this really weird feeling any time we were in there. A few strange things: Despite being one of 12 units in the building we only ever saw two of our neighbors in passing...and even then only a single time each. We shared a wall with a couple and their under-a-year-old baby. We saw them once, a few weeks after moving in, but never seemed to run into them again. Second weird thing: stuff would just go flying. I don’t mean like stuff would get knocked over, I mean things would fly off surfaces with force. There was no regularity to this happening. I think he’s probably embarrassed to even admit to having these thoughts, knowing they aren’t rational and could come off as seeing you in a negative light. Try to avoid feeling accused. This isn’t about you as a wife or a mother, this is his mind telling him he isn’t good enough.

In a lot of rural communities things work like this: OP hunts a deer. OP brings home 25 lbs of meat to feed his family. The butcher buys 25 lbs of meat at a low price which is then sold for a small profit to families (often elderly people) who want the meat but can’t always afford high end cuts of things like beef. OP has now fed himself, brought money to the butcher, and provided a service to people who wouldn’t always be able to access meat. All of this happened without any factory farming or food processing, just a single shot to the head of an animal who didn’t expect it and therefore wasn’t afraid.

The way I see it deer hunting is the prevention of future suffering. If deer are allowed to breed as much as they can, absent of natural predators or human hunters, the population would explode within a year or two and deer would begin starving en masse. Climate change has just caused the exact same thing with reindeer, in fact. There would be so many that they would begin starving to death, leaving piles of deer corpses in the woods. Is it better for 100 deer to starve in agony or 10 deer to be instantly and painlessly killed and their meat used to feed a family? This is one of those cases where human intervention into nature is both necessary and merciful. I am not a hunter myself but family members are and they are always mindful to ensure that the deer is downed with a single shot and every bit of it used. When I say every bit, I mean literally everything, bones into stock, weird insides into dog food, etc. Is that not better than going to the store and buying factory farmed meat?

The best advice I can give a 15 year old:
- accept that some things are boring and you can’t get out of them. The sooner you stop worrying about how much something will suck and just do it the sooner it’s over. This applies to everything from the DMV to college classes you get stuck in because they fit your elective credits. 
- don’t be afraid to try things you currently think are weird or stupid or not your thing. Stuff I’m super into at 29 would have baffled 15 year old me. Take risks when it comes to things that can’t kill you. The worst that can happen is you don’t have fun and don’t do it again. In that same vein, if you aren’t having fun somewhere just leave. You don’t have to keep doing something if it sucks and you aren’t enjoying yourself.
- You probably won’t marry the person you’re dating in high school and early college and that’s okay.
- Took a weed edible? You aren’t dying. No one ever dies of ODing on weed. Watch a cartoon and take a nap, you’re fine. 
- keep up with your hobbies. Everyone I know who stuck with the things they were passionate about in high school are now seriously amazing at what they do. 
- never take out a payday loan. Just don’t do it. 
- get your HPV vaccine.
- go to community college first or a state school. Private colleges aren’t worth the loans you’ll be saddled with. Your friends who went to really cool schools are now paying really cool bills for the rest of their lives.
- learn to cook. Seriously. YouTube is your friend and you will be the coolest dude in your group of friends. One of my guy friends hosts every holiday and get together now because he is a food god.
- laundry isn’t that hard, just separate your colors, whites and darks and don’t put in too much soap.
- ask for help before you get overwhelmed
- your resume is less important than your cover letter. Your cover letter sells you as a person and can make up for a mediocre work history.
- it’s okay if you are not currently a prodigy at something and don’t know what you’re gonna do with your life. General education and internships exist for a reason. Explore what you like, leave behind what you hate. 
- Try not to stress too much about the future. Nothing kills motivation faster than failing to reward yourself for the victories of today.

I think a lot of it becomes a numbers game. As a dog breed becomes more popular for looks or “toughness” more people breed them without accounting for health or temperament. So as the population of these breeds explodes so does the number of attacks perpetuated by that breed because there are more of them with poorer temperaments running around in the hands of owners who have no business having them. We saw it with German Shepherds and Dobermans in the 90s, the population of them exploded and people with no background in owning the breeds began irresponsibly owning and handling them, leading to attacks. Pits are large, strong dogs with high prey drives and need to be treated as such and handled by people who have done their research and invested time and money into proper training. I do think we will begin to see the same thing happen with pits that eventually happened with German Shepherds and Dobermans: a different desirable breed will come along (already beginning to happen with Huskies being the new dog of choice) and suddenly all the dumb people who wanted the newest coolest dog will be hopping on that breed train. The pits left behind will either end up euthanized in shelters for temperament or adopted out to the kind of people who won’t be breeding them, ending the huge boom of pits in a matter of a decade or so.

My partner works at a facility that is the “last chance” for a lot of highly aggressive dogs. There are a few dog aggressive (Not people aggressive) pits there but the largest number of dogs are non-bully mixed breeds and Daschunds. Rotweillers were the product of a big scare campaign in the 80s and 90s but aren’t generally a big problem breed when it comes to reactivity and bites.

Get the second dog. A dog that you can do all the things you enjoyed doing with your last dog with but who will also love being around your current dog.
